Photograph: San Francisco department of animal care and control San Francisco San Francisco pitbull rescued after two days trapped in railway tunnel Pup named Roo, who ran away from home, was found curled up next to rail track – and was ‘thrilled’ to be rescued Uwa Ede-Osifo Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.07 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A two-year-old pitbull who ran away from home braved two days in a dim San Francisco railway tunnel before being rescued. Caltrain operators spotted the pup named Roo on his first day in the tunnel. Looking at the dog’s unmoving body, they had assumed he had been fatally struck by a train, according to a recent social media post from the San Francisco animal care and control shelter. On the second day, after Roo was seen moving, police officers set out on foot in the tunnel with a flashlight. View image in fullscreen Caltrain operators helping the pup named Roo. Photograph: San Francisco Department of Animal Care & Control They found Roo, lying curled next to a rail track, and led the dog out of the dark into the light of day. “He was terrified at first, then was thrilled to be rescued,” the animal shelter wrote in the post. The pup is a recent adoptee, who ran away after being “spooked”. Fortunately, Roo was microchipped. He has since been reunited with his owner. The San Francisco area has rallied around other dogs in distress as of late. Menlo Park firefighters rescued a missing dog that was found swimming in the San Francisco Bay, as seagulls followed in pursuit. https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/worl.text: The Danube River has dropped to unusually low levels in Budapest, exposing long-hidden remains from the Second World War. This has revealed the bodies of two Wehrmacht soldiers, a German military motorbike and several wartime objects that had stayed buried in mud for about 80 years.According to Euro News, the discoveries were made along the riverbed near Batthyany Square, on the Buda side of the Hungarian Parliament. The area is reportedly usually filled with moored boats.The two soldiers were recovered from the muddy riverbed by the German War Graves Commission, known as Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgraberfursorge. The mud had preserved both the bodies and their identity discs in unusually good condition.Alongside the human remains, recovery teams also found German Tellermine 35 anti-tank mines, a military decoration, a petrol can and what experts believe is a DKW NZ 350-1 military motorbike. The finds offer a rare look at the final days of the war in Budapest.The German military motorbikeThe most striking discovery was the German military motorbike recovered from the middle of the Danube. It was found on 2 August near the harbour at Batthyany Square, close to the Hungarian Parliament.The motorbike was lifted by the Institute and Museum of Military History. Based on its design, experts believe it is a DKW NZ 350-1 model, which was widely used by the German military during the Second World War.According to the German War Graves Commission, the model was known at the time for being especially robust and reliable.The objects are believed to have remained on the riverbed since the final stages of the war, when fierce fighting took place in and around Budapest.The two soldiersThe recovery of the two soldiers has drawn particular attention because of the remarkable condition of their remains. The German War Graves Commission said a reburial specialist travelled to Budapest to carry out the exhumation with Hungarian experts. The bodies had been preserved by the thick harbour mud, which also protected their identity discs.According to the organisation, the mud at Batthyany Square is mixed with gas oil. This created conditions that slowed the decay of both human remains and metal objects buried beneath it.The reburial specialist said the petroleum in the mud helped preserve the identity discs so well that the letters and numbers on them remain clearly legible after around 80 years underwater.This is important because identity discs were the main form of military identification during the war. Every Wehrmacht soldier carried an identity disc made in two matching halves. If a soldier died, one half of the disc was removed and sent to the Wehrmacht information office in Berlin so the military could officially record the death and inform the soldier's family.In the case of the two soldiers recovered from the Danube, both halves of each identity disc were still together. The German War Graves Commission said this means their deaths were never officially reported to the information office. The preserved discs may now help authorities establish their identities before they are buried.The German War Graves Commission is responsible for locating, recovering and reburying German war dead in many countries where battles took place during the Second World War.Hungary was an ally of Nazi Germany during most of the Second World War and became a major battleground in the final months of the conflict. Soviet and Romanian forces surrounded Budapest in late 1944, while German and Hungarian troops defended the city. The fighting continued into February 1945 and left large parts of Budapest heavily damaged.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

https://www.stripes.com/theaters/europe/.text: Menu Mobile App Download the app Today's ePaper Read the latest print edition Rewards for readers Archives/Library Subscribe Log in Newsletters Follow Stars and Stripes Facebook X LinkedIn YouTube Threads Europe Baltic officials downplay alarm after CIA director’s surprise Moscow visit By DEVIN KLECAN STARS AND STRIPES Published August 27, 2026 · Baltic officials said Thursday that their assessments of the threat from Russia had not changed following reports that CIA Director John Ratcliffe warned Moscow against escalating tensions with NATO allies during an unannounced visit this week. “We must remain vigilant, but Estonia’s threat assessment has not changed,” Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in a statement . “The best deterrent is a united and strong NATO and the clear understanding in Moscow that the Alliance is prepared to defend every inch of Allied territory.” Latvia’s defense chief Kaspars Pudans, meanwhile, also downplayed the imminent threat, telling the news outlet Delfi that if there were signs of danger “I wouldn’t be sitting here.” The comments follow reports that Ratcliffe used the visit on Tuesday to warn Russian officials against actions that could escalate tensions with NATO. Ratcliffe specifically raised concerns about potential Russian actions against Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, Politico reported , citing two people familiar with the meeting. Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Ratcliffe warned Russia not to attack any NATO member countries. Neither the U.S. nor Russia has disclosed what was discussed during the Tuesday visit, which was the first time a CIA director has visited Russia in about five years. The meeting happened weeks after The Wall Street Journal reported on U.S. intelligence assessments warning that Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve with a limited attack, such as a cyberattack or a small-scale land incursion, on an allied country in the next few years. In a radio interview Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump described Ratcliffe’s mission as “semi-routine” and suggested it could help efforts to end the war in Ukraine. In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Ratcliffe talked with Russian intelligence officials but did not meet Putin. The Russian president has been briefed on the meeting, Peskov added. U.S.-Russia relations have been severely strained by Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the stalled diplomatic efforts to end the conflict. There has also been friction over Russia’s reported support for Iran during its war with the United States. According to Politico, Ratcliffe conveyed a desire for Moscow to stop sharing weapons and defense technology with Iran and advised Moscow against “overreacting” if Russia is affected by recently tightened U.S. sanctions on Tehran. The surprise visit caused speculation online after public flight-tracking data showed a U.S. Air Force Boeing C-17A Globemaster III flying from Riga, Latvia, to Moscow’s Vnukovo International Airport. Toward the end of 2021, then-CIA Director Bill Burns visited Moscow to warn against the Kremlin’s planned invasion of Ukraine. Months later, the full-scale invasion began. “One thing should be obvious: it would be a grave mistake to assume that Russia’s leadership will fundamentally alter its strategic objectives (re Ukraine, Europe or Iran) because of messages delivered by the CIA director,” said Mark Mihkelson, Chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee of the Estonian Parliament, in a post on X. The CIA, White House, Pentagon and U.S. Air Force declined to comment or did not respond to requests for comment. http://www.philippinetimes.com/news/2793.text: Polands Fort Trump could cost up to $4.4 bn National Security Bureau RT.com 27 Sep 2026, 05:32 GMT+10 The project could be approved by the end of the year, according to Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka Poland could pay up to 17 billion zloty ($4.4 billion)to house a permanent US military base on its territory, the presidential National Security Bureau (BBN) has said. The project, which is currently being discussed with Washington, involves a facility that could house 5,000 troops, the agency told the newspaper Rzeczpospolita this week. Warsaw offered to host a permanent US base during President Donald Trump's first term in 2018, proposing to name the facility 'Fort Trump.' Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski confirmed this week that a deal on the base was nearing completion. Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who traveled to the US this week for the talks on the base among other things, stated that the final decision rests with Trump and that she did not expect it to be made before the review of the posture of US forces, which is expected to be finalized in November or December. According to the BBN, the base could be completed in 2029 under "optimal conditions." Under Trump, Washington has pressed European NATO members to boost defense spending and take on more responsibility for arming Ukraine while the US concentrates resources on competing with China. The US is also widely expected to scale back its military presence in Europe as part of this strategy shift. America still considers Poland a "model ally," according to US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, the man behind the US policy shift that has since become known as 'NATO 3.0.' Sobkowiak-Czarnecka also told journalists this week she had heard "many warm words from the American side acknowledging our preparedness and motivation." The US already has a permanent Army garrison and command headquarters in the city of Poznan, although most of the 10,000 US troops stationed in the country serve on a rotational basis. According to Deputy Defense Minister Stanislaw Wziatek, this number could grow to 15,000, with 5,000 stationed permanently at the new base. Warsaw has been one of Kiev's most ardent supporters in its ongoing conflict with Moscow. It also serves as a key logistics hub for delivering Western military aid to Ukraine while also bordering the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad to the northeast. Tensions between Moscow and Warsaw recently flared as Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski vowed to inflict a swift defeat upon Russia in case of a direct clash with NATO. "If Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly," he stated in mid-September, prompting Nikolay Patrushev, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to warn that Poland could "cease to exist" within days if it undertakes military action against Russia and forces Moscow to use its full arsenal. https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text: Jessie Buckley accepts the award for best actress at the Oscars in March. ‘I feel so proud being part of this community’ … Jessie Buckley. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Jessie Buckley accepts the award for best actress at the Oscars in March. ‘I feel so proud being part of this community’ … Jessie Buckley. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images Movies Jessie Buckley suggests film industry gives too much weight to Oscar campaigns The actor, who won the Academy Award for best actress this year, was speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.38 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jessie Buckley has questioned whether the film industry places too much emphasis on Oscar campaigns at the expense of nurturing emerging talent, suggesting there may be greater potential in supporting film-makers at grassroots level. Speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards in London, the actor was responding to comments by John Malkovich, who said Oscar campaigns were now the only way to get audiences into cinemas . “I think there’s truth in that,” Buckley told the Guardian. “You’ve got to take responsibility for sharing your work. It would be so easy to just go and film and then hide. I wish we could all do that. But I don’t think that’s how it works any more.” Buckley, who has made predominantly independent films, said the industry’s reliance on film promotion affected not just actors and directors but the wider workforce. “I feel so proud of being part of this community – this affects so many people’s lives. Crews, marketing, everybody. And if you don’t support it, you’re not going to have a job,” she said. “Maybe we’ve given that too much weight. I wonder if there’s more potential in nurturing at a grassroots level than giving so much weight to a marketing Oscar campaign.” Four emerging UK film-makers were named recipients of this year’s BFI and Chanel film-makers awards, each receiving £20,000 to develop their work. They were announced at a ceremony at Claridge’s in London on Wednesday, with Buckley and Gwendoline Christie joining a jury that also included BFI CEO Ben Roberts, Edward Enninful and Marie-Louise Khondji. We need to support the next generation. I want to know what they’ve got to say, what their world looks like Buckley called for greater support for film-makers working outside established industry structures, pointing to the success of films “made on shoestring budgets”, including Obsession and Backrooms . “People went to see them because of their quality, not because of the IP or what was deemed successful beforehand,” she said. “It’s essential that we support up-and-coming young film-makers. It would be completely selfish if we didn’t. At some point we want to pop off this earth, and we need to support the next generation. I want to know what they’ve got to say, what their world looks like.” The four winning films explored subjects including political protest, racial profiling, female solidarity and family trauma. View image in fullscreen Jury members Gwendoline Christie and Jessie Buckley (centre) with, from left: Rich Felgate, Olive Nwosu, Imran Perretta and Rachel Taparjan. Photograph: James D Kelly Rich Felgate, director, producer and cinematographer of We, the Hated, was recognised for his documentary about Just Stop Oil protesters and the personal consequences of participating in a polarising movement. The jury described the film as “urgent and brave”. Buckley said it had prompted her to reconsider the role of protest in society. “In our world at the moment, protest seems like such a dangerous act, when historically it’s been essential to democracy,” she said. “It realigned me and reminded me of how important protest is, and how we can misunderstand the people within that. That we need to understand more and need films like that more.” Olive Nwosu won for Lady, her feature debut set in Lagos, which follows one of the city’s few female taxi drivers as she becomes drawn into the world of a childhood friend who has become a sex worker. The jury praised Nwosu’s cinematic ambition and her handling of challenging material. Imran Perretta was recognised for Ish , a black-and-white coming-of-age film set in Luton’s South Asian and Middle Eastern community. It follows two 12-year-old best friends whose relationship is tested after a police stop and search. The jury praised its exploration of racial profiling and the experience of being British while being treated as an outsider. Rachel Taparjan won for Something Familiar, her debut feature documentary about her search for her missing sisters after being adopted from Romania and brought to the UK as a child. The jury praised the film’s “naked, unselfconscious revelation of self”, saying it had stayed with them longest. Christie said the strength of this year’s field meant the jury had concluded it “couldn’t just select three winners”. The awards, which celebrate creative audacity and ambition, have run since 2022. Previous recipients include Harry Lighton, whose film Pillion won best British independent film at the British independent film awards in 2025, and Savanah Leaf, who received the 2024 Bafta for outstanding debut by a British writer, director or producer. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/10/31/varg.text: Menü Kereső Blikk: Varga Judit eladta a Magyar Péterrel közösen épített balatonhenyei házat Belföld frissítve Joób Sándor Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Varga Judit eladta azt a balatonhenyei házat, amit házasságuk idején Magyar Péterrel közösen építettek, majd a válásuk után a volt igazságügyi miniszteré lett, írja a Blikk . Arról korábban mi is beszámoltunk, hogy Varga Judit már régebb óta árulta a közel 2000 négyzetméteres telken álló 233 négyzetméteres házat 299 millió forintért. A Blikk most azt írja, az új tulajdonosok ugyanúgy vigyáznak rá és szépítgetik, mint ahogy azt Varga tette. A korábbi hirdetés szerint a ház „korszerű technológiát és kimagasló kényelmet kínál” belülről, míg külsőleg „hűen követi a balaton-felvidéki tájjellegű építészet hagyományait.” Többek között az is kiderül, hogy az „ingatlan teljesen okosított: a hűtés-fűtés, a riasztórendszer, a kapunyitás, a kamerarendszer és a napelempark távolról, okostelefonról vezérelhető.” A telket 2013-ban vette Magyar és Varga, amikor még házasok voltak, 2017-ben pedig családi otthonteremtési kedvezményt igényeltek és kaptak a ház építésére. Ebben az időben azonban nem itt éltek, a 10 millió forintos támogatást pedig nyaralóra nem kaphatták volna meg. A balatonhenyei ház egyébként nem is minősül annak, hivatalosan családi házról van szó. Mivel nem éltek ott életvitelszerűen a támogatást követő 10 évben, 2023-ban Varga Judit miniszterként visszafizette a 10 millió forintot . Az ingatlanról 2021-ben számoltunk be részletesen . Varga 2024-ben közzétett vagyonnyilatkozatából az is kiderül, hogy a váláskor a ház mellett két üres balatonhenyei telken is osztozkodtak, és az egyik Magyar Péteré lett.
